hints: Start from the bullet points given - think about what makes an animal cheap and easy to keep in a lab for hundreds of individuals.
Think about what you need for genetics - the ability to choose which male mates with which female, and to see results over many generations quickly.
Think about why results in flies matter for people - what does similarity in development and cell signalling genes allow researchers to do?
walkthrough:
Think Like a Geneticist - What Do You Need?**
You need an organism that is cheap to house, easy to breed on purpose, and gives you lots of data fast. Fruit flies are tiny, about 3 mm, so thousands fit in small vials with simple sugar food.

Link Life Cycle to Genetic Power**
Because males and females are easily distinguished, you can set up particular crosses. A female lays hundreds of eggs in a few days and the life cycle is short, so you get large sample sizes and many generations in weeks. That makes ratios reliable and selection experiments possible.

Why Still Relevant Today**
Many development and cell signalling genes are similar to human genes. That means findings about inheritance, mutation and gene function can be used as a model to research human conditions such as cancer.

Final answer: Small size so kept in small space at low cost with low maintenance; parents can be selected for specific matings/crosses; short life cycle with hundreds of eggs gives many offspring/generations in short time; genes similar to humans so can research human diseases e.g. cancer / neurodegenerative disease.

Remember the two genes are on different chromosomes, so they assort independently. What four gamete types will each F1 produce?

walkthrough:
Work Out Dominance First**
Wild type grey long crossed with black short gives 100% grey long F1. That only happens if grey is dominant to black and long is dominant to short. So let A = grey, a = black, B = long, b = short. Parents are AABB x aabb, so all F1 are heterozygotes AaBb.

Get the F1 Gametes by Independent Assortment**
Genes are on different chromosomes, so alleles segregate independently in meiosis. Each AaBb parent can make four gamete combinations in equal numbers: AB, Ab, aB, ab. Put these across the top and down the side of the Punnett square.

Fill the Punnett Square and Read Phenotypes**
Combine row and column to get 16 F2 genotypes, e.g. AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb all look grey long, AAbb and Aabb look grey short, aaBB and aaBb look black long, aabb looks black short. Counting gives $9$ grey long : $3$ grey short : $3$ black long : $1$ black short.

Present It the Cambridge Way**
Always show symbols key, parental phenotypes and genotypes, gametes, full Punnett, then list offspring phenotypes with the ratio underneath. That layout earns each marking point separately.

Final answer: Symbols: A = grey, a = black; B = long wing, b = short wing. F1 phenotypes: grey long x grey long; F1 genotypes: AaBb x AaBb. Gametes: AB, Ab, aB, ab x AB, Ab, aB, ab. Punnett gives 16 genotypes including AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb, AAbb, Aabb, aaBB, aaBb, aabb. Offspring phenotypes: grey long, grey short, black long, black short. Phenotypic ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

hints: A grey long F2 could hide recessive alleles - think about which partner would let any hidden recessive allele show up in the offspring.
Focus on body colour first - what offspring would you see if the F2 was AA versus if it was Aa when crossed to a black-bodied fly?
Apply the same logic to wings - what offspring tells you the F2 must be Bb, and what result proves it must be BB?
walkthrough:
Why You Need a Test Cross**
A grey long F2 could be AABB, AaBB, AABb or AaBb. You cannot tell by looking because dominant alleles mask recessives. Crossing to the fully recessive aabb means the tester only gives ab gametes, so the offspring phenotype directly reveals the gametes made by the unknown F2.

Read the Body Colour Result**
If any offspring have black bodies, the F2 must have given an a allele, so it is heterozygous Aa. If all offspring have grey bodies, no a was given, so it is homozygous AA.

Read the Wing Length Result**
The same rule applies independently. If any offspring have short wings, the F2 gave a b allele, so it is heterozygous Bb. If all offspring have long wings, it gave only B, so it is homozygous BB.

Final answer: Carry out test cross with double homozygous recessive (black body short wings, aabb). If some offspring black then F2 is Aa, if all grey then F2 is AA. If some offspring short-winged then F2 is Bb, if all long-winged then F2 is BB.
